calls.head: The Hurricanes’ goalie is in for some dangerous shots
calls.body: The Canadiens’ shots are some of the most dangerous in the league, and the Hurricanes are the league’s worst at preventing dangerous ones. Look for plenty of good chances.
calls.call: The Canadiens’ average shot has at least their usual 6.9% chance of going in.
calls.nums: Montréal 1st for shot quality (a 6.9% chance of scoring on the average shot) · Carolina 32nd for preventing dangerous shots
calls.cite: Style fingerprint · this season blended with last · 2 and 3 games this season
calls.happened: Montréal’s average shot had a 6.5% chance of going in, against their usual 6.9%.

calls.head: The Canadiens can’t afford to take penalties
calls.body: The Canadiens’ penalty kill is near the bottom of the league, and the Hurricanes’ power play is near the top of the league. Discipline matters more than usual for the Canadiens tonight.
calls.call: The Hurricanes’ power play creates at least their usual 8.1 expected goals per 60.
calls.nums: Carolina 6th for power play (8.1 expected goals per 60) · Montréal 26th for penalty kill
calls.cite: Style fingerprint · this season blended with last · 3 and 2 games this season
calls.happened: Carolina’s power play created 4.3 expected goals per 60 in 6:11 of 5-on-4 time, against their usual 8.1, and scored 1 goal.

calls.head: Two of the league’s heaviest-hitting teams
calls.body: The Hurricanes and the Canadiens are both among the league’s heaviest hitters, even after adjusting for each arena’s scorer. Keep your head up.
calls.call: The two teams’ combined hit score reaches their usual 108.
calls.nums: Hit score (100 is league average): Carolina 109 (7th), Montréal 107 (10th)
calls.cite: Style fingerprint · this season blended with last · 3 and 2 games this season
calls.happened: The two teams’ combined hit score was 140, against their usual 108 (100 is league average, after adjusting for the arena’s scorer).
calls.beyond: Carolina’s hit score in the close stretches of the game was 153, against their usual 109 (100 is league average, adjusted for the arena’s scorer). A team strays this far about once every 10 games.

MTL.head: We gave Montréal only a 40% chance, and it went the way we feared.

CAR.head: We gave Carolina a 60% chance, and Carolina delivered.

surprises.head: Carolina buried Montréal in shots
surprises.body: Carolina took 73% of the 5-on-5 shot attempts (adjusted for score and venue). From how these two usually play, Carolina would expect about 57%. A team strays this far about once every 60 games.

surprises.head: Montréal tried a different line
surprises.body: F. Xhekaj, J. Anderson, J. Evans played 6:59 together at 5-on-5, a trio that isn’t one of Montréal’s usual lines.

story.head: The Hurricanes beat the Canadiens
paras: Taylor Hall scored twice, opening the scoring early in the first. Five different Hurricanes scored. The game was tied three times.

The score was fair. Replay this game’s chances a hundred times and the Hurricanes win about seven in ten. By our Swing measure, Phillip Danault had the best night of anyone, even in a loss. The Canadiens tried a line they hadn’t used before: Florian Xhekaj, Josh Anderson and Jake Evans.

items.text: Whether the Canadiens keep that line together at home against Nashville on Thursday.
One of the preview’s three calls held.
